content: Adverse reactions to the Haemophilus b conjugate vaccine, HIBERIX, have been documented through clinical trials and postmarketing surveillance. Below is a detailed description of these reactions: 1. Clinical Trials Experience: Adverse reaction rates observed in clinical trials may not directly correlate with those seen in broader clinical practice due to varying conditions under which trials are conducted. Seven clinical studies involving 1,008 children evaluated HIBERIX as a booster dose following primary vaccination with various Haemophilus b conjugate vaccines. These included HIBERIX (not approved for primary series in the US), vaccines manufactured by Sanofi Pasteur SA, Merck & Co., Inc., and Wyeth Pharmaceuticals Inc. (no longer licensed in the US). The studies were conducted in Europe, Canada, and Latin America, with the mean age of children at booster vaccination ranging from 16 to 19 months. The majority of participants were white, and approximately half were male. HIBERIX was administered alongside non-US formulations of vaccines such as INFANRIX® (DTaP), KINRIX® (DTaP-IPV), or PEDIARIX® (DTaP-HBV-IPV). Some subjects also received DTaP-HBV (not licensed in the US) concomitantly with HIBERIX. 2. Solicited Adverse Events: In a German open-label, multicenter study, 371 children received a booster dose of HIBERIX with DTaP-HBV-IPV. Adverse events were recorded for four days post-vaccination. Local reactions at the injection site included redness or swelling greater than 20 mm (Grade 3) and pain severe enough to cause crying when the limb was moved (Grade 3). Fever was defined as ≥100.4°F (≥38.0°C) rectally or ≥99.5°F (≥37.5°C) axillary, oral, or tympanic. Grade 3 fever was defined as >103.1°F (>39.5°C) rectally or >102.2°F (>39.0°C) axillary, oral, or tympanic. Grade 3 fussiness was characterized by persistent crying that could not be comforted, and Grade 3 symptoms were those that interfered with normal daily activities. 3. Serious Adverse Events: Two serious adverse events were reported among 1,008 subjects within 31 days of booster immunization. One child developed bilateral pneumonia nine days post-vaccination, and another experienced asthenia following accidental drug ingestion 18 days post-vaccination. 4. Postmarketing Experience: Since the vaccine's market introduction in 1996, voluntary reports of adverse events have been collected. These include serious events and those with a plausible causal connection to HIBERIX. However, due to the voluntary nature of these reports, the frequency and causality cannot be reliably established. General Disorders and Administration Site Conditions: Extensive swelling of the vaccinated limb and injection site induration. Immune System Disorders: Allergic reactions, including anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions, and angioedema. Nervous System Disorders: Convulsions (with or without fever), hypotonic-hyporesponsive episodes, somnolence, and syncope or vasovagal responses to injection. Respiratory, Thoracic, and Mediastinal Disorders: Apnea. Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue Disorders: Rash and urticaria. These findings highlight the importance of monitoring for both common and rare adverse reactions following vaccination with HIBERIX.
